name: Palate expanders (adult)

lead: Palate expanders widen the upper jaw. In adults, miniscrew-assisted rapid palatal expansion (MARPE) or surgically assisted expansion is used for a narrow upper jaw, and looksmaxxers seek it for a wider midface, broader smile and easier breathing.

A screw-driven appliance anchored to the teeth, mini-implants in the palate, or both is turned to separate the midpalatal suture so new bone forms in the gap. Adults often need bone anchorage or surgical help because the suture has matured. Trials report skeletal expansion and some airway changes in selected patients; systematic reviews describe the evidence in late adolescents and adults as limited, and trials rarely measure facial attractiveness.

paras: It is delivered by orthodontists or oral surgeons: an appliance is fitted, adjusted at home over weeks, then held in place while bone fills in, usually followed by braces. Total treatment runs many months.

Reported effects include pain, speech changes, a gap between the front teeth, tongue sores, periodontal changes and variable success in adults. Surgical versions carry operative risks, and the work needs a qualified orthodontist.

angle.text: Adult expansion widens the upper jaw, which can broaden the dental arch, midface and smile. It is an established orthodontic procedure studied for narrow upper jaws and breathing; its effect on overall facial appearance has not been tested.

lead: Palate expanders are orthodontic devices that widen the upper jaw (maxilla) so that the upper and lower teeth fit together and the upper arch is broader. They are most often used in children and adolescents, whose midpalatal suture is still open. Adult versions, such as miniscrew-assisted rapid palatal expansion (MARPE) and surgically assisted expansion (SARPE), are used for transverse maxillary deficiency in patients whose palatal suture has matured [1].

For appearance, the proposition is a wider upper arch: a broader smile with more teeth showing, more room for the teeth, a broader midface and, as users hope, improved support for the cheeks and eyes. Looksmaxxing communities discuss adult expansion for these reasons and for easier nasal breathing [2]. Orthodontic trials measure skeletal width, tooth movement, airway and pain rather than attractiveness, and systematic reviews describe the efficacy evidence for MARPE in late adolescents and adults as limited [3].

Mini-implant-supported designs were developed in the 2010s and are now the subject of case reports, imaging studies, randomized trials and reviews [2][4][3][5]. This article covers the family of devices used in adults; the MARPE entry covers the bone-anchored appliance in detail.

paras: Rapid palatal expansion (RPE or RME) uses a key-turned screw that moves the arms of the appliance, typically about half a millimetre to a millimetre a day until the crossbite is corrected, followed by roughly three to six months of retention while bone fills the midline gap [1]. Slow expansion turns the screw at about a millimetre a week over eight to ten weeks, and Wikipedia describes it as giving roughly equal dental and skeletal change [1]. Devices include the Haas, Hyrax, Quad Helix, bonded expanders and the Bionator, and they can be tooth-supported, bone-supported or both [1].

MARPE anchors the appliance to the palate with two to four mini-implants, which allows expansion in some young adults with fused sutures and gives more skeletal and less dental change than tooth-borne devices [1][5]. A variant, the Maxillary Skeletal Expander (MSE), places four bicortical mini-implants in the posterior palate [2].

Surgically assisted expansion (SARPE) involves an oral and maxillofacial surgeon cutting the midpalatal suture before the expander is activated, and is used when the palate has matured; an orthodontist attaches the appliance and finishes the case [1]. Wikipedia states that most adults, and men in particular, may need a surgical assist for consistent results [1].

Wikipedia traces palatal expansion to the nineteenth century: Westcott reported applying mechanical forces to the maxilla in 1859, and Emerson Angell published the first paper on expansion, a screw placed in a 14-year-old girl, in Dental Cosmos in 1860 [1]. The idea was opposed by J. H. McQuillen in 1889 and revisited by Goddard in 1890 and Landsberger in 1910 [1]. Andrew Haas reintroduced his expander in the United States in 1956, Biederman introduced the Hyrax in 1968, Cohen and Silverman the bonded expander in 1973 and Robert Ricketts the Quad Helix in 1975 [1].

Mini-implant-supported designs followed in the 2010s. A 2014 finite element study modelled stress in the nasomaxillary complex, a 2016 case report treated a 19-year-old with MARPE, and a 2017 clinical article by Brunetto, Sant'Anna, Machado and Moon credits Won Moon and colleagues at UCLA with MARPE as a less invasive alternative to SARPE [2].

Orthodontists generally describe expansion as indicated when the upper arch is narrower than the lower, a crossbite is present or the airway is narrow; Wikipedia gives a guide of at least about 4 mm of difference measured between the first molars [1]. Expansion in adults is slower and more uncomfortable than in children, and results depend on suture maturity and age [1][6].

In looksmaxxing discussions, adults ask whether an expander is possible at their age, whether a clinic will prescribe one when the orthodontist sees no clinical need, and how MARPE compares with jaw surgery. One poster, treated with braces, reported two orthodontists telling him his palate was adequate while he wanted a fuller smile, wider lips and an upturned eye look, and asked whether MARPE or a segmental maxillary osteotomy would suit [7].

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of MARPE in patients aged 16 and older assessed success rate, skeletal and dental expansion, treatment duration and side effects, and described the evidence on efficacy as limited [3]. An umbrella review of four systematic reviews and a 2023 update on expansion in nongrowing patients compare conventional, surgical and miniscrew-assisted approaches.

A randomized trial of 40 adolescents and young adults compared conventional rapid expansion with MARPE using low-dose CBCT: suture separation occurred in 90 percent of conventional and 95 percent of MARPE patients, with greater nasal and maxillary width after MARPE [5]. A trial of 60 post-pubertal patients reported suture separation in 100 percent with MARPE and 86.7 percent with a Hyrax expander and a higher ratio of skeletal to dental change with MARPE. A 2025 randomized trial of 30 late adolescents and young adults found sutural opening in 53 percent with conventional expansion and 60 percent with MARPE, and larger improvements in nasal airflow after MARPE.

Studies of adults add age effects: in one CBCT series success was 83.3 percent at ages 15 to 19, 81.8 percent at 20 to 29 and 20 percent at 30 to 37 [6]. A comparison of MARPE and surgically assisted expansion in postpeak adolescents and adults found more parallel skeletal expansion with MARPE and more buccal tipping with the surgical approach [8]. A CBCT study of 14 young adults measured expansion of 5.5 mm at the crowns and 2.0 mm at the basal bone [4], and a follow-up of 24 patients reported stable outcomes one year after expansion with some relapse [9].

A multicentre controlled trial in adults with obstructive sleep apnea examined MARPE's effects on sleep and quality of life, a controlled trial of 20 adults found upper airway volume rose 11.6 to 16.1 percent, and a randomized trial of 48 adults found micro-osteoperforation reduced pain during MARPE expansion. The studies' main outcomes are skeletal width, dental effects, airway and pain measures rather than facial attractiveness.

Reported effects of palatal expansion include speech changes and a lisp, extra saliva, pain and headaches when the screw is turned, tongue sores, a gap between the upper front teeth, and changes to bone and periodontal tissues such as bone fenestration and tooth extrusion [1]. The zygomatic buttress limits posterior expansion, so expansion tends to be greater at the front [1]. Older studies cited in the same source found that a third to a half of expansion could be lost before stabilization [1].

Research reports that MARPE can fail to open the suture in some patients, which is why success rate is an outcome in reviews, and tipping of anchor teeth and thinning of buccal bone are measured in trials [3][5][4]. Surgical versions carry operative risks and are performed by surgeons [1].

Wikipedia states that posterior expansion and expansion of the nasal aperture are considered important in treating obstructive sleep apnea and that expanders can help the airway after dental extractions [1]. MARPE trials report airway volume gains, improved nasal airflow and, in one multicentre trial, improvements in sleep measures.

Looksmax.org has many threads about palate expanders and MARPE, with users asking about age limits, outcomes and the choice between MARPE and jaw surgery. One thread title asks about palate expanders for aesthetic benefit even when orthodontists disagree, comparing MARPE with a two- or three-piece maxillary osteotomy [7]. A thread asks whether expanders are worth it at 20, with replies that tongue posture practices remain effective at that age [10].

For younger teens, a post lists approaches said to expand the maxilla without an appliance, including tongue posture, nasal breathing, chewing tougher foods and swallowing technique [11]. Mewing proponents claim sustained tongue pressure widens the upper jaw; orthotropic practitioners use expanders under professional supervision mainly in children, and mainstream orthodontic bodies find no credible evidence that mewing reshapes the jaw, according to one encyclopedia.

Related options include MARPE, SARPE, segmental maxillary osteotomy and Le Fort-type jaw surgery discussed alongside them [7]. Tooth-borne expansion in adolescents is reviewed with MARPE in a 2022 systematic review, which concluded that MARPE was more predictable than a Hyrax expander with fewer side effects.

lore.intro: Adult palate expansion is discussed on looksmax.org as a non-surgical way to widen the midface and smile, with frequent questions about age limits and whether an orthodontist will agree to prescribe one [7][10][7].
